title: ARIA 101 for UXers
intro: ARIA is the set of cues assistive technology reads aloud. Rule one: don't use it if semantic HTML does the job.

learn.title: Four layers that matter
learn.text:
**Anchor navigation** — `aria-current` answers “where am I?”. One per set: page, step or location.
**Clarify meaning** — `aria-labelledby` and `aria-describedby`, reusing visible text.
**Reveal state** — `aria-expanded` on the toggle itself, with optional `aria-controls`.
**Signal change** — `role="status"` (polite) or `role="alert"` (urgent).

try.q: Which attribute answers “where am I in this set?”
try.explain: One per set — page, step or location.

learn.title: What the gaps sound like
learn.text:
In a financial-dashboard study, every screen-reader participant hit what one called **“an invisible wall”**.

• Missing `aria-current` → “Am I on step two or three?”, and clicks on the page they're already on
• Missing labels → “What is this button supposed to do?”
• Missing `aria-expanded` → they press Enter, nothing seems to happen, and they assume it's broken

try.q: A participant presses Enter on a toggle and assumes the product is broken. What is missing?
try.explain: Without the state, nothing in the announcement changes.

left.label: What users hit
items: “Am I on step two or three?”

learn.title: Live regions and care
learn.text:
A live region must **exist in the DOM before the update** and must not be `display:none`.

Marking everything `assertive` overwhelms people — reserve it for urgent messages.

For form errors: set `aria-invalid` and link the message with `aria-describedby`.

Researchers can hear these gaps in sessions before users hit them in production.

try.q: Why must a live region exist before the content updates?
options: Because screen readers cache the DOM
Because CSS transitions interfere with it
try.explain: A region created at the same moment as its content is usually missed.
